html:
The Tibetan script is the alphabet used to write Tibetan. It was adapted from an Indian script in the 7th century, in the time of the Tibetan Empire.

Tradition says King Songtsen Gampo sent his minister Thonmi Sambhota to India to study writing, and that Thonmi came back and designed the script and its grammar. Some scholars doubt the story or date the script a little earlier, but all agree that it comes from a Brahmi based script of north India, close to the Gupta script of the time.

It has thirty consonant letters and marks added above or below them for vowels. Words are split into syllables by a small dot. Its spelling has hardly changed in over a thousand years, so modern spoken Tibetan no longer matches how words are written.

The script carried a huge body of translated Indian Buddhist texts, gathered later into the Kangyur and Tengyur canons. It is also used for Dzongkha, the language of Bhutan, and other Himalayan languages. Under the Yuan dynasty, the Tibetan monk Phags pa adapted it into a new script for all the languages of the Mongol empire.
sum: The Tibetan script is the alphabet used to write Tibetan. It was adapted from an Indian script in the 7th century, in the time of the Tibetan Empire.
